Welcome to the fictional world of Kynsra! This is a completely made-up language, and any resemblance to any real language is purely coincidental. Let’s imagine you are in a cafe and want to order a meal.

Server: Vytha qixen fa rosyn? (What would you like to eat?)
You: Ki jomzan mifal. (I would like the soup.)
Server: Ki vymet dor kopza? (Would you like bread with that?)
You: Ni, ki sifud ryndir. (No, just water.)
Server: Hal vytha qixen hyn mifal? (Would you like the soup now?)
You: Ah, hyne ron (Yes, please)
Server: Rax, ki jomzan werio. (Okay, the soup is coming.)
You: Rin, fa elltam. (Thank you, have a good day.)

In Kynsran grammar, verbs generally come at the beginning of the sentence. “Vytha” means “would you like,” “ki” is the subject pronoun for “I,” “jomzan” means “to eat,” and “mifal” is “the soup.” “Ni” means “no,” “sifud” means “water,” “ryndir” means “just,” and “dor kopza” means “bread with that.” 

To express a question in Kynsra, you can indicate it either with word order or by adding “hal” at the beginning of the sentence. “Rax” means “okay,” “hyne” means “yes,” “hin” means “no,” “fa” is a preposition used to indicate the purpose of the verb, “elltam” means “good day.”

Hope you enjoyed a little taste of Kynsra!

Sure, here's a sample conversation in Kynsra for booking a holiday to Arvada and purchasing a language course for learning Arvadan:

You: Fyoq naqikin rygtalva Arvada?
(Can I book a holiday to Arvada?)
Travel Agent: Ah, rygtalva Arvada. Es ani arynavon laquomu, tozha ki tytza elegon. (Ah, a holiday to Arvada. It's a beautiful place, and you will enjoy it a lot.)
You: Rin, ki te tilysto livo vana es efa?
(Yes, can you tell me about the available flights there?)
Travel Agent: Es ferlaqa oquixan mikuzox yador. Ki te ti orvoro legiz hynge livon. (There are direct flights on Fridays. I can book one for you today.)
You: Rax, ki fevymon. Ni tynzalza lymaq tytza, ki talmunahan yadynad Arvada.
(Okay, let's do it. I want to learn Arvadan, can I purchase a language course for that?)
Travel Agent: Ah, ki orvoro oqozto Arvada! Es tilysto melzor. Ya talthoza ki vidazon namas goqstar. (Ah, you want to learn Arvadan! That's great. We have a very good language course here.)
You: Rin, fa qalmaquom.
(Yes, please.)

In Kynsra, "fyoq" means "can I," "naqikin" means "to book," "rygtalva" means "holiday," and "Arvada" means "Arvada." "Es" means "it is," "ani" means "beautiful," "arynavon" means "place," "laquomu" means "you will enjoy it," "tozha" means "and."

"Tilysto" means "available," "livo vana" means "flights there," "te" is used as a subject pronoun for "can you tell me." "Ferlaqa" means "direct," "oquixan" means "on," "mikuzox" means "Fridays," "orvoro legiz" means "book one today."

"Fevymon" means "let's do it," "tynzalza" means "to learn," "lymaq" means "language," "talmunahan" means "I want," and "yadynad" means "Arvadan."

"Tilysto" means "available," "melzor" means "good," "talthoza" means "we have," "vidazon" means "course," and "namas goqstar" means "very good." "Qalmaquom" means "please."
